title: Serbia's Vucic Concedes to a Student Movement, Algeria Sends Troops Abroad for the First Time Since 1973, and Jordan Bombs Syria's South
subhead: Three developments reset different maps on the same day: fourteen years of Serbian strongman rule end at the ballot box, Algeria breaks a five-decade ban on foreign deployments to secure energy assets in Niger, and Jordanian jets strike inside Syria without Damascus's consent.

sections.heading: Serbia: Vucic Concedes After 14 Years
sections.body:
Aleksandar Vucic admitted defeat on Sunday night in Serbia's snap parliamentary election, ending fourteen years in power. According to Serbia's election commission, with 97% of polling stations counted, the student-led Student List took 2.25 million votes (52.7%) against 1.67 million (39.2%) for Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party, the BBC reported. Vucic told supporters at SNS headquarters that it was 'clear we have lost these elections'.

The movement that beat him grew out of the November 2024 collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station, which killed 16 people and triggered two years of anti-corruption protests. Vucic called the snap vote himself; he had served two presidential terms and was campaigning to return as prime minister. Student List lead candidate Ilija Srdanovic told BBC Serbian: 'This will be a free state.' Radomir Saicic, another of the movement's candidates, said Serbians had shown that 'no force can forever overpower a people who have decided to take their destiny into their own hands.'

What remains unsettled is who actually governs. The Student List has no obvious leader and its members have never held office; the movement is now preparing talks on forming a government, according to the Guardian. Vucic remains a force in parliament with roughly a quarter of the seats, and the SNS retains control of much of the state apparatus.
sections.whyItMatters: Serbia sits at the junction of EU accession, Russian energy dependence and Balkan stability. A government run by inexperienced anti-corruption activists is an unknown quantity for Brussels, Moscow and the region — and Vucic's 105-seat bloc gives him real capacity to obstruct.

sections.heading: Algeria Breaks a 53-Year Taboo and Deploys to Niger
sections.body:
Algeria's parliament approved sending troops to Niger — its first foreign military deployment since it sent forces to Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war. The upper house voted 148 of 174 senators in favour in an emergency session on Sunday, per AFP, and the lower house followed, the BBC reports. The timing and size of the deployment have not been announced.

Algerian senator Belkacem Boulghiti framed the mission narrowly: 'We are not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger, but for a mission to secure economic infrastructure.' The troops are expected to protect energy facilities in northern Niger near the Libyan border, including a planned pipeline that would carry Nigerian gas north through Niger to Algeria. The deployment follows a visit to Algiers by Niger's defence minister and uses a 2020 constitutional provision never before invoked.

The move caps a fast repair of relations that had broken down. Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers in 2025 after Algeria shot down a Malian drone, and Algeria had condemned the 2023 coup that brought General Abdourahamane Tchiani to power. Tchiani visited Algiers in February 2026, and in late August President Abdelmadjid Tebboune sent fighter jets to help suppress a coup attempt in Niger, along with four donated helicopters. Sonatrach has separately signed an exploration deal with Niger's petroleum ministry in the Kafra region, where Reuters reported two wells are estimated at 168 million and 100 million barrels.
sections.whyItMatters: Algeria has spent decades refusing to project force abroad, and that posture was a core part of its non-alignment identity. Sending troops into the Sahel to guard gas infrastructure turns Algeria into a security actor in a region where Russia's Africa Corps, jihadist insurgencies and Western retrenchment are all competing for influence — and it links Algerian energy security to Niger's stability.

sections.heading: Jordan Bombs Southern Syria, and Damascus Denies It Agreed
sections.body:
Jordanian aircraft struck targets in southern Syria on Monday in retaliation for Friday's gun attack on a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, which killed at least nine people. Syria's Civil Defence said the strikes hit four sites in rural Deraa and Suweyda provinces and killed seven people — three men, a woman and three children — with five of the dead from one family hit in a tent in the village of Al-Tai, Al Jazeera reported.

The two governments give incompatible accounts of the operation. Jordan's Armed Forces said it hit 'hideouts' of armed groups and that the strikes were launched 'in coordination with the Syrian government'. Syria's foreign ministry called the operation a 'treacherous attack' conducted 'without prior coordination or notification' and said it had opened an investigation. Syria then closed the Nassib crossing, the only passenger and commercial land link between the two countries.

Jordan had already arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law in the village of Al-Jadeeda after a three-hour shootout, according to a Jordanian government source quoted by Al Jazeera. King Abdullah II had pledged the 'harshest penalties'.
sections.whyItMatters: Jordan has spent the past year trying to stay out of regional wars. Striking inside Syria is a new posture, and the dispute over whether Damascus consented points to a deeper problem: the Syrian government's inability to control the south, which borders both Jordan and the Israeli-occupied Golan.

sections.heading: Iran Talks: Tehran Says Washington Is Not Serious, and a Ship Burns off Iraq
sections.body:
Iran accused Washington of not being serious about negotiations, according to Al Jazeera's live coverage, as Gulf shipping risks rose again: the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported a vessel on fire 63 nautical miles southeast of al-Faw, Iraq.

The more consequential development was in Tehran. Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Iran's president and the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, in the first joint meeting of its kind, Iranian state television said. A statement carried by Fars said the participants agreed to keep talking to strengthen cooperation among the four countries. Saudi officials have not confirmed any agreement; deputy foreign minister for public diplomacy Rayed Krimly characterised the visit as part of Mecca Joint Defence Agreement efforts at de-escalation and support for Qatari and Pakistani mediation.

Pakistan's Munir had visited Tehran the previous week, where Iranian officials told him there would be no talks with Washington until Tehran's demands were met, per Iranian media. Earlier mediation produced an interim agreement in June that collapsed within weeks. Saudi Arabia intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Sunday as Houthi attacks continued.
sections.whyItMatters: The Mecca pact — signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan in August, with an attack on one treated as an attack on all — was built as a counterweight to Iran. Its members are now in Tehran negotiating directly with the Iranian security establishment. That is either de-escalation or the pact being repurposed as a channel; Riyadh is not saying which.

sections.heading: Ukraine: Kyiv Hit Hours Before an Oleshky Truce, and Romania Names a Russian Hand
sections.body:
Russian strikes on Kyiv late on Monday killed one person and wounded eight, with mayor Vitali Klitschko reporting damage to medical facilities including an intensive care unit. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said ballistic missiles struck the grounds of a university campus: 'The missiles hit very crowded areas, and there is not a single military facility nearby.' The attack came hours before a truce was due to begin at 3am local time in Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson region, intended to let aid into a city with severe food, water and medicine shortages. No end date, monitor or operational detail has been published.

Zelenskyy also said Kyiv has waited nearly a month for US defence secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on Patriot and NASAMS missile supplies, and that he had ordered his team to raise it with Washington again.

Separately, Romania said a network 'coordinated' from Russia was behind a fire near an arms factory in Brasov on 14 September. Two Belarusians and a Ukrainian resident in EU countries were involved, authorities said; two were detained in Germany while preparing similar acts and the third is at large in Poland. The Guardian notes that at least eight cargo ships have been hit off Romania and Bulgaria in the past three weeks, with 34 sailors reported dead or missing.
sections.whyItMatters: The Oleshky truce is the first localised ceasefire of this phase of the war, and it began with a mass-casualty strike on the capital. The Brasov finding, plus the shipping attacks, shows the sabotage campaign against NATO's Black Sea flank has moved from deniable to prosecutable.

sections.heading: Also Watching: Israel Votes Today Under a Hebron Operation, and Merz Goes to Asia
sections.body:
Israel holds its general election on Tuesday with the military operation in Hebron still running. The UN says more than 3,000 people, including 200 babies, were ordered to leave the Deir Baha neighbourhood; Hebron municipality figures cited by DW put displacement across the city at nearly 2,000. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of 'the spectre of ethnic cleansing looming ever larger', and Human Rights Commissioner Volker Turk called the operation collective punishment. A UN report released Monday accused Israel of war crimes in the West Bank; Israel's foreign ministry called it 'a propaganda document detached from reality'. Israel is also closing all West Bank land crossings on election day, per DW.

Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz began a five-day Asia tour in Singapore, heading to Japan on Wednesday for talks with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and the German-Japanese Business Summit, with 30 business leaders in tow. President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is in China at the same time. DW quoted Waseda University's Ben Ascione saying Tokyo would welcome German military deployments to the region.

In Ethiopia, the Orthodox Church says more than 60 people were killed in attacks on Christians across three areas of Shirka district in Oromia, with 20 houses burned; a local official blamed the Alliance for Survival, a new coalition that includes the Oromo Liberation Army, which has not commented.
sections.whyItMatters: An Israeli election held during a mass-displacement operation in Hebron will shape whether the West Bank policy continues or is reversed. Merz's Asia trip and Steinmeier's China visit in the same week signal Berlin hedging its supply chains and security ties away from a single reliance on Washington.

bottomLine: Vucic's loss is the day's biggest change: a student movement born from a train-station disaster now holds 52.7% of the vote and no governing experience, in a country that straddles EU accession and Russian energy. Algeria's vote to send troops to Niger ends a 53-year refusal to deploy abroad, turning a gas-pipeline route into a military commitment in the Sahel. Jordan striking southern Syria while Damascus insists it was not consulted shows how thin state control has become along that border. None of these resolves quickly; the Iran file did produce one concrete shift — Mecca pact members sitting with Iran's security chief in Tehran — but without a Saudi confirmation of what was agreed.
